issues.legal_issue: A person claiming pre-emption solely by consanguinity cannot obtain a pre-emption decree when the statutory right based on consanguinity has been invalidated.
material_facts: The claimant in the pre-emption suit relied on her relationship to the former owner and was not a co-sharer.
The pre-emption decree was entered without a finding establishing a superior right other than the asserted kinship.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not claim a right of pre-emption based on consanguinity.
issues.legal_principle: In Atam Prakash v. State of Haryana, the Court held that the consanguinity-based categories in Section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, were unconstitutional. The Act’s provisions preserving pre-emption rights for other qualifying classes did not preserve a right based solely on kinship.

predicates.preemption_proceeding: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking to exercise a right of pre-emption.
predicates.claimant_relied_on_kinship: The claimant based the asserted pre-emption right on a family relationship to the former owner.
predicates.claimant_not_a_co_sharer: The claimant did not hold a co-sharer’s interest in the property.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a pre-emption proceeding relies on kinship rather than a co-sharer’s interest, the kinship-based claim is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption decree cannot take away the property rights of a purchaser who was a necessary party but was omitted from the proceeding and was not given an opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: The property had been transferred to the purchaser by registered sale deeds before the pre-emption suit was brought.
The purchaser was in possession, and the pre-emption claimant knew of the purchase.
The purchaser was not joined in the pre-emption suit, yet the decree was used to assert rights over the property against the purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was a necessary party, and a decree could not be passed in the purchaser’s absence to take away the purchaser’s rights in the property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, treats registration of an instrument as notice of the transaction and actual possession as notice of the possessor’s title. Article 300-A protects the right to property, which cannot be taken away except in accordance with law. The Court also emphasized that the statutory right of pre-emption is weak and that the procedure for asserting it must be followed. In Shyam Sunder v. Ram Kumar, the Court described the right of pre-emption as a statutory right to substitute the pre-emptor for a stranger purchaser.

rule.if: preemption_proceeding and prior_registered_purchase and purchaser_in_possession and purchaser_excluded_from_proceeding

predicates.preemption_proceeding: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking to exercise a right of pre-emption.
predicates.prior_registered_purchase: The property had been transferred to a purchaser by a registered instrument before the pre-emption proceeding.
predicates.purchaser_in_possession: The purchaser was in actual possession of the property.
predicates.purchaser_excluded_from_proceeding: The purchaser was not joined in the proceeding and was not given an opportunity to be heard.

issues.definition: When a pre-emption proceeding concerns property already purchased by a registered instrument and the purchaser in possession is excluded, a decree cannot take away that purchaser’s property rights.

issues.legal_issue: A consent decree obtained through collusion and suppression of material facts is void when the parties to it cannot convey the interest that the decree purports to affect and the omitted purchaser is a necessary party.
material_facts: The original purchasers had transferred their rights and interests in the property to another purchaser before the pre-emption suit.
The claimant brought the pre-emption suit against only the original purchasers, omitting the later purchaser.
The consent decree recognized a superior pre-emption right without a finding establishing its basis.
Only part of the stated sale consideration was deposited in court, and the remaining amount was paid to the original purchasers, who had already transferred their interests.
The Court found that the circumstances showed collusion and suppression of material facts in obtaining the decree.
issues.conclusion: The purported consent decree was void ab initio because the original purchasers could not convey an interest they no longer held, the necessary purchaser was absent, and the decree had been obtained through collusion and suppression of material facts.
issues.legal_principle: A decree obtained by fraud on the court through suppression of material facts cannot stand. A consent decree cannot validly transfer an interest that the consenting parties no longer hold, and a suit cannot proceed in the absence of a necessary party whose rights are affected. The Court applied these principles alongside Sections 19 and 21 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, which address notice to pre-emptors and suits for pre-emption.

predicates.consent_decree_in_preemption_proceeding: The parties resolved a pre-emption proceeding by a consent decree.
predicates.original_purchasers_had_transferred_thei: The purchasers named in the proceeding had transferred their interest in the property before the decree was made.
predicates.later_purchaser_excluded: The later purchaser whose rights were affected was not joined in the proceeding.
predicates.decree_obtained_by_collusion_or_suppress: The decree was obtained through collusion or by concealing material facts from the court.

issues.definition: When a consent decree in a pre-emption proceeding is obtained after the original purchasers have transferred their interest, with the later purchaser excluded and through collusion or suppression, the decree is void.
